articles.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
articles.content: We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below. Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs. Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks. We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card . When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models). articles.title: E-means: Outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs
articles.content: An order of magnitude less epochs Across a large range of scales and datasets , e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs, in 1.2 to 3 epochs. Measured end to end, that is a 10–45× wall-clock reduction on GPU against the state-of-the-art Lloyd implementation (Flash-KMeans [2] ), and 8–15× on CPU against Faiss [1] . Speed and quality usually trade against each other in k-means, while e-means achieves both better speed and loss. The k-means problem Given a fixed dataset of n points X = {x 1 , ..., x n } ⊂ R d and an integer k , the k-means problem is to find k centroids C = (c 1 , ..., c k ) minimizing the mean squared distance between each point and its nearest centroid: \[ \mathrm{MSE}(X, C) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|x_i - c_{a(i)}\|^2, \qquad a(i) = \arg\min_{j \in \{1,\dots,k\}} \|x_i - c_j\|^2 \] \[ \mathrm{MSE}(X, C) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|x_i - c_{a(i)}\|^2 \] \[ a(i) = \arg\min_{j \in \{1,\dots,k\}} \|x_i - c_j\|^2 \] It's a static dataset, unlike codebook learning inside VQ-VAEs, where the distribution to cluster is constantly moving. The e-means project The goal of e-means is to provide a modern optimization rule for the k-means problem. We started this project from the following observations: k-means is one of the rare problems in machine learning where full-batch optimization is still widely used. Mini-batch k-means methods in the literature exist [3] , [4] , [5] , but are mostly based on the MacQueen update rule, released in 1967. Modern deep learning offers optimization tools that can enhance mini-batch methods. For e-means, we chose to do mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages [6] , which we found to be most efficient for the k-means problem. Contrary to previous mini-batch approaches, e-means requires no hyperparameter tuning because it automatically sets the batch size and step size with scaling laws (see Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws ). In addition, e-means improves the initialization and the dead-cluster revival strategy, adds a cosine-scheduled decay rate, and introduces a finalization stage that reduces the training loss for a negligible runtime penalty at the end of training. e-means is highly parallelizable, and comes with specialized kernels that translate its algorithmic advantage into wall-clock speedups. Moving-average updates Each mini-batch updates every cluster's count and sum. The centroid is their ratio. old centroid new centroid batch mean No hyperparameter tuning Everything is derived from scaling laws. log n, log k, log T Start and finish Novel initialization and finalization methods. The run ends on each cluster's exact last-epoch mean. start exact mean Cosine scheduling The step α anneals from α 0 to 0.1 α 0 , as a learning rate does. α₀ 0.1 α₀ Dead-cluster revival Clusters with size below a threshold are revived by splitting a large cluster. below threshold large cluster split in two Specialized kernels GPU kernels fuse the nearest-centroid assignment,

articles.title: Payments Canada announces launch of Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system
articles.content: The new system will enable participating financial service providers to clear and settle payments in real time, providing a made-in-Canada platform for future innovation and prosperity. OTTAWA, ON, November 9, 2026 – Payments Canada today announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR). This new national payment system will transform day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers by enabling instant speed and settlement, real-time cash-flow visibility and data-rich messaging through existing banking and payment channels. The launch of Canada’s RTR marks a major milestone in modernizing the critical infrastructure that underpins Canada’s economy and future growth. The RTR will enable participating members, including financial institutions, credit unions and payment service providers, to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time for their customers, 24 hours a day, every day of the year. “A stronger, more productive economy relies on modern financial infrastructure that can match our ambition,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail lays the foundation for a more dynamic and competitive digital economy, driving innovation, expanding choice and creating new opportunities for Canadians while positioning our country for long-term growth.” “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country,” said Susan E. Hawkins , President and CEO, Payments Canada. “As a national asset that’s designed specifically for our country, the RTR gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on. By collectively leveraging this rail, our ecosystem will unleash its full potential, enabling our members to build capabilities that drive innovation, resilience and growth for businesses and consumers across the nation.” Ron Morrow, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne and Susan E. Hawkins The RTR will drive significant cost savings and economic growth in Canada over the next decade. The C.D. Howe Institute projects that, with its functionalities at launch, the RTR will generate up to $14.5 billion in cost savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques, and reduced float (the period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient). Extending beyond these cost savings, the RTR is expected to generate $16 billion in economic gains , growing to $27 billion as new functionalities are introduced over time. “The Real-Time Rail is an important step in modernizing Canada's payment infrastructure and ensuring it keeps pace with Canadians' evolving needs,” said Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. “The Bank will oversee the system so that it operates safely and reliably while ensuring Canadians can benefit from innovations in financial services.” Owned and operated by Payments Canada, and built in collaboration with delivery partners CGI, Deloitte Canada, IBM

articles.title: Semi-transparent, colored cadmium telluride photovoltaic panels in agrivoltaics
articles.content: Vegetable farms and solar farms both need lots of sunlight and open space. But how do we divide our limited lands between these two priorities? One elegant solution is to put crops and solar panels on the same land—and share the broad spectrum of incoming sunlight between them. A new study in Cell Reports Physical Science does this with photovoltaic cells that are semi-transparent: They capture some wavelengths of sunlight to make electricity, while letting the wavelengths most critical to photosynthesis pass through and reach the plants below. The new study suggests that broccoli can be grown in the magenta shade of these solar panels —without sacrificing the harvest. Agrivoltaic schemes— putting plants and solar on the same land – could help us avoid clearing more land for human use. Climate studies suggest that this might work especially well across a wide sunbathed swath of the United States, from Texas up to Nebraska and west to California . Devoting just one percent of U.S. farmland to agrivoltaics could cover up to 20 percent of the nation’s electricity needs. But traditional photovoltaic panels are opaque—and by shading plants, they can reduce crop yields. So engineers are trying to create new photovoltaic cells that divide the spectrum of sunlight between plants and electricity generation—similar to how governments segment different frequency bands for television, radio, cell phones, and other uses. A 2020 study looked at panels that allow red wavelengths, critical for photosynthesis, to pass through—while harvesting green and blue wavelengths to make electricity. Basil grown under these panels produced similar yields, while spinach yields decreased. But the researchers estimated that by selling both electricity and crops, farmers growing spinach could generate 35 percent more income from the same land. In the newest study, scientists evaluated a different kind of semi-transparent panel that lets most red and some blue wavelengths pass through—casting a magenta light on the plants—while converting much of the rest to electricity. Broccoli cultivated under them grew more slowly, requiring an additional 25 days for harvest, but produced roughly the same yield. Meanwhile, these magenta sunscreens improved the microclimate below, reducing the “vapor pressure deficit”—a measure of when plants need to halt photosynthesis to avoid excessive water loss. This may have improved the plants’ efficiency in converting sunlight into plant biomass, which increased by 2.8- to 4.5-fold compared to unshaded plants. The shaded plants’ levels of macronutrients such as calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus were either higher than or similar to unshaded plants, while levels of some micronutrients such as iron, copper, and zinc were slightly lower. This was only a preliminary study. Future studies should look at larger plots, farmed across multiple seasons, and in different locations with varying climate and sunlight. articles.title: Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game
articles.content: LLMs can make complete multi-level games that are fun. TL;DR - Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game from a bunch of drawings, and it's a lot of fun. You can try it here . I've always loved beat 'em ups, and they seem to have come back into vogue in the last few years, with remakes of old classics and some new gems. When my nephews visit, I use it as an excuse to try them out. Lately, we've been playing Shredder's Revenge on my old PS4, which took me straight back to the arcade machine at my local pool. One day, my younger nephew, Aiden, came to me with a proposal. Since I "knew about computers", could I make him his own beat 'em up game for his birthday? He had already drawn up the game design docs. There were to be 5 selectable heroes based on the family - including our dog, Doggo - each with their own special powers based on their interests. He had 12 bosses drawn up and a loose outline of a story. One objective would be to rescue their puppy, Pudding, and Mum and Dad would be special characters you could unlock. Heroes The Battle Wagon The villains, numbered 1st to 12th At the time - around January 2026 - building an indie game from scratch was a pretty unreasonable ask for a birthday present, and I did warn him to temper his expectations. Still, I thought it would be a fun exercise to test the agentic tools at my disposal. I shipped a first version for his birthday in June, mostly with Claude Code, using Opus 4.8 and Fable 5, and a side-scrolling template courtesy of AIOriented.dev . It worked, but it wasn't worth playing for more than a couple of minutes. The June version. Aiden was appreciative, but it clearly wasn't the game he'd imagined. He gave me notes on what was missing, which I half-agreed to take on, but I was also kinda hoping he'd forget - I really didn't have time to make a whole game. Unfortunately, he did not forget. Every time I saw him, he asked about the game. Enter: Fable 5.2 I was lucky enough to get an early look at Claude Fable 5.2 , and was told to try it on "my most ambitious use case". articles.title: How Much Energy Does Building Distro Packages Use
articles.content: Some metrics When I set up the infrastructure for Casuarina Linux I repurposed an AMD AM4 system with Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core CPU (105W TDP) and 32Gb of DDR4 RAM as the build server. I set it up in our laundry, connected it via a smart plug, and reset its counters. Over the course of the project I would regularly pull package updates from Chimera Linux , build and install them locally, and then push them to the repo, which would trigger Buildbot to build and publish them. 💡 All prices are quoted in Australian dollars You can select a different currency, which will use exchange rates from the time of writing. Currency: AUD BRL CAD CHF EUR GBP HKD INR JPY KRW PLN RUB SEK USD The project ran from 30 March 2026 to 8 November 2026 (a bit over 7 months) the total energy used was 98.4 kWh. My electricity plan is a 100% renewable plan (meaning they offset the non-renewable parts) and costs AU$0.33 kWh. Ignoring the daily service fee the cost of that electricity is AU$32.47 . Since it turned out I was the only one doing package updates I kept the builder off when idle. When there were packages to build I’d hit the power button (on the machine, not the smart plug) and some time later when it was done I’d press it again to shut it down. This was pretty beneficial as the idle draw was about 55W. The number of package builds was around 5000. SELECT COUNT(name) FROM logs WHERE name LIKE 'pkg:%'; from the Buildbot state.sqlite yields 5201, however that’s probably slightly inflated due to rebuilds/packages that failed to build on the first try. The actual usage is likely more than double the 98kWh figure as all packages were built on my desktop machine first, before pushing to the repository for the builder to pick up. That machine is an AM5 system with AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D 16-Core CPU (170W TDP), 64Gb DDR5 RAM. Additionally our house has rooftop solar, and where possible I would kick off builds during the day so there was a better chance of using the solar. That would have reduced the actual cost, but I have no way to measure the specific amount. The slowest package by far to build was Chromium, taking just shy of 4 hours to complete. For comparison Firefox takes about 50 minutes. Power draw measured by the smart plug when the builder was fully loaded is about 193W. So 4 hours at 193W is 0.77kWh, which means a Chromium build costs about 25 cents. Overall it cost a bit under AU$5 a month (ignoring solar, and my workstation) to build all the packages for a Linux distribution. That’s not too bad I think.
articles.summary: 作者用 Ryzen 9 5950X 搭建 Casuarina Linux 构建服务器，通过智能插座统计构建发行版软件包所耗电量。

articles.title: Microsoft are rejecting your mail
articles.content: On Friday morning, we became aware that a significant amount of email to Microsoft-run mail systems was being rejected. This included mail to hotmail.com and outlook.com. The messages were being rejected with the following message: 550 5.7.1 Message rejected: Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC Auth Records We checked our logs, and found that we’d seen this message over 500 times on Thursday, but not once before that. The affected messages all had completely valid SPF and DKIM , but did not have a DMARC record. We added a DMARC record with a “none” policy to some of the affected domains, and sure enough, mail was then accepted again. A quick fedi-survey confirmed that we were not alone. DMARC records are a way of publicly stating what you want recipients to do with email that claims to be from your domain, but which doesn’t pass verification checks (DKIM or SPF) and thus is potentially forged. Your DMARC policy can be one of the following: reject – recipients should reject mail that doesn’t pass DKIM or SPF. This is the real purpose of DMARC: if you’re confident that all legitimate outbound mail is properly authenticated, you can tell recipients to assume that anything else is forged, and bin it. quarantine – recipients should treat such mail as suspicious. none – your domain has no policy on what to do with mail that doesn’t pass DKIM or SPF. Publishing a policy of none is effectively the same as not publishing a policy at all. Microsoft are now rejecting mail without a DMARC policy, but accepting mail with a policy of none . This is a massive and pointless change in their policy for incoming mail, made with no notice whatsoever. Last year Microsoft, introduced a policy that required domains sending more than 5,000 messages per day to have a DMARC record. This change was announced in advance . This latest change appears to be completely unannounced, which makes us wonder if it was even intentional. Of course, trying to contact Microsoft in order to resolve mail issues such as this is futile. Update: apparently it wasn’t intentional, but they haven’t figured out how to roll it back yet. We’ve just applied p=none DMARC records to a large number of our customers’ domains. We generally try to avoid making unsolicited changes to DNS zones, but in this case we feel that it is the best option. If you’re in contact with Microsoft users affected by this, please encourage them to complain to Microsoft; it’s very likely that they are losing other legitimate email from other providers because of this unannounced change. Better still, encourage them to move to an email provider that is pro-active in investigating email deliverability issues .
articles.summary: 大量发往微软邮件系统的邮件被以缺少 SPF/DKIM/DMARC 认证记录为由拒绝，影响 hotmail 和 outlook 用户。

articles.title: Let’s Talk About Why all This OT Stuff is Connected
articles.content: It’s been a really bad month (and year) for OT cybersecurity. From a wave of new, high-impact vulnerabilities, to attacks on supermarket refrigerators , to attacks on blood banks , we’ve been left shorthanded and reeling. And that’s on top of months of attacks against water utilities . Through all of this, I keep seeing the same comment from seasoned enterprise cybersecurity people, and as someone dealing with these cases on the front line, I find it very frustrating. They express intense shock that these systems are accessible via networks at all, then ask why they can’t just be disconnected. It goes something like this: This is just one example, and I’m genuinely not trying to bash the OP. I’m certain they’re a very competent, experienced IT person, and I understand their frustration. But the situation is far more complicated than it looks, and calling the people who support and purchase these systems incompetent won’t fix it. So let me try to explain why so much OT, ICS , and IIoT is exposed, and which systems are in the worst state. How We Got Here Before we can talk about the current state of OT, we need to go back 15 to 20 years to discuss IT/OT convergence. Before then, industrial devices and network infrastructure were often highly bespoke, heterogeneous technologies engineered by vendors. Most communication was serial-based, protocols were custom, and even device firmware was developed in-house. A Rockwell system looked nothing like a Siemens system. When you purchased a system, it was designed, deployed, and supported by that specific OEM. They supplied the replacement parts. They trained the technicians and installers. This got expensive, and it slowed down logistics, not just for parts but also for labour. So clever engineers and businesspeople looked at the IT landscape and had an idea. Using Windows computers as human-machine interfaces, and commercial Ethernet to encapsulate serial traffic, would be much cheaper to buy, replace, and train technicians to support. Over the years that followed, systems became a mix: lower-level PLCs and RTUs down at Level 1, and above them, numerous devices that were far more familiar to IT staff. Unfortunately, they were also familiar to hackers and hacking tools. This was the first change in exposure, and it was really just a loss of security by obscurity. The next change was the homogenisation of OEM deployments. To deploy and support large-scale systems more efficiently, most industrial vendors started producing very uniform deployments of technology across the Purdue Model , in very static architectures. Network maps and addressing can look incredibly similar between deployments, even across verticals and countries. Once again, this was the most financially and logistically efficient solution. Unfortunately, any savvy cybersecurity professional can see how this lends itself to more scalable attacks, and even to automating parts of those attacks with tools and agents. The Age of Remote Connectivit

articles.title: Terminal2Shell: Critical flaw grants instant shell access on every major OS
articles.content: ACTIVE EXPLOITATION IN THE WILD · ESTIMATED 2+ BILLION AFFECTED DEVICES · NO PATCH AVAILABLE What is Terminal2Shell? Terminal2Shell is a design-level vulnerability in terminal emulators. When a terminal is launched, it immediately spawns a shell process and connects it directly to the user's keyboard. From there, the attacker can issue arbitrary commands with the full privileges of the logged-in user. Researchers have confirmed that the shell will execute any command typed into it, including commands that delete files, install software, and modify system configuration. In some cases, the shell has been observed executing commands the user typed themselves . Proof of concept We are releasing a working proof of concept below. It is fully weaponized. Click inside and start typing. Try help . victim@localhost: ~ (pwned) The page you are reading now has a shell in it. Close the tab if you are concerned. Exploitation steps Open a terminal. There is no step 2. Exploitation requires local access, a working keyboard, and the ability to locate the Terminal application. Threat intelligence indicates all three are widely available to attackers. Indicators of compromise If you see any of the following characters followed by a blinking cursor, your system is actively compromised: $ % > ❯ # A # prompt indicates the attacker has obtained root . Disconnect from the network, then from society. Mitigations No vendor patch is available. Until one is released, we recommend the following compensating controls: Do not open terminals This is the most effective mitigation. Note that many developers report opening terminals "for work," which security teams should treat as a red flag. Close terminals immediately after opening them Partial mitigation only. Reopening the terminal reintroduces the vulnerability. Type slower Reduces commands per minute and therefore attack throughput. Remove the keyboard Effective, but the on-screen keyboard is a known bypass. Set SHELL=/bin/false Fully remediates the issue. Also fully remediates your ability to use the computer. Disclosure timeline 1971 Vulnerable code ships in Unix v1 as the Thompson shell. 1979 Bourne shell released. Vulnerability preserved with full backwards compatibility. 1989 Bash released. Name confirms the attack is intentional. 2009 zsh adoption grows. Now the shell is also pretty, which researchers believe lures more victims. 2026 Researchers notify all vendors simultaneously. 2026 Vendors respond: "That is what a terminal is." 2026 Researchers register a domain, design a logo, and contact the press. Coordinated disclosure considered complete. FAQ Am I affected? If you own a computer, yes. If you own a phone, you are affected but have not found the terminal yet. Is this being exploited in the wild? Yes. Telemetry shows millions of developers exploiting Terminal2Shell every day, often dozens of times per hour. Some have set it to open automatically on login. articles.title: unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world
articles.content: unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world November 7 2026 I've always had a soft spot for this particular car brand. Our family has owned a few of them over the years, and they've served us incredibly well. In 2023, I bought a new four wheel drive/SUV from them, and it was the first time I had access to their connected car platform. Having looked at platforms like this before ( previous works ), I was sceptical about how secure they really were. I suspected there was something there, but life kept getting in the way of actually looking. This July, I collaborated with Sam Curry to take a look at the security of a major automaker's connected car systems. Throughout this post, I'll refer to them simply as "the automaker". When you typically think of car hacking, it's often easy to jump into the hardware side of things, but my background sits pretty squarely in compromising internet-facing web applications and infrastructure. Regardless of all the hardware bits and bobs, it all connects back to some service that, by design, has to be reachable from the internet. The journey started with a simple question: what infrastructure does the app talk to when I remotely unlock my car? To work this out, I downloaded the APK and decompiled it, eventually reconstructing the API requests that were being made. Going through the code, the primary point of contact seemed to be assets under *.redacted-telematics.com.au : dartExecutor.executeDartEntrypoint(createDefault, CollectionsKt.r(gson.toJson(new GlobalConfigParams(false, g11, com.redacted.app.xcapp.a.f69866f, "X", str)), new Gson().toJson(new ApiConfig("https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au" ... Almost every part of the consumer application called back to redacted-telematics.com.au . What else existed under this domain? Running connected car infrastructure can be quite complex, and managing it requires a mix of admin tools, staging, dev, and QA environments, to make sure that customers get a clean experience. Whether all of that should be sitting on the public internet, available to anyone willing to do some basic reconnaissance, is a different story. One asset caught my attention more than the others. admintool.redacted-telematics.com.au returned a page titled TEST HARNESS. Who can resist a subdomain with admintool in it? Visiting this subdomain presented a very plain and grey login screen, which didn't exactly ooze quality, given it presented a logout button before we'd logged in. I love that most single-page applications ship their entire JavaScript bundle even when all they need to render is a login page. Sure, some more modern frameworks split out JavaScript files so that they only serve what is necessary, but in this case, we could comb through the large JavaScript bundle to understand what this "admin tool" actually let you do. articles.title: Sure mate, buy me a bloody coffee
articles.content: I don’t usually get involved in the internet reply-fest du jour , but this time I thought I’d give it a go. It involves coffee, just in case you wondered. My sister-in-law gave me this espresso cup. It’s pretty cool. BTW: I’ve used a bit of the antipodean vernacular in this post. You have been warned. There was a bit of a kerfuffle last week on the IndieWeb about whether or not people should have a “buy me a coffee” (or equivalent) link on their blog. The argument of the article that sparked the debate being that this is rampant capitalism, everything is getting monetised these days, it’s not going to cover your hosting costs, hosting doesn’t cost much anyway, so why bother, and please just stop. Well, that was my impression. I can understand the perspective. It seems that everything on the internet is being monetised in some way or form. “Don’t forget to like and subscribe!”, “Join my newsletter!”, “Read my Substack!”, “Buy from my affiliate links!”, “And now a word from this video’s sponsor…”, etc., etc., etc., ad nauseam. And I get that, I really do. There’s just so much advertising everywhere that it’s hard to get away from. I agree: it’d be nice if there were islands of quiet in the online world where no call to monetary action existed. And I get it that personal blogs don’t strictly need a virtual tip jar. My guess is that very few people are making any real money from them. But it’s not about the money. It’s more about recognition for the hard work that writing entails and about being seen for that work and someone going “Hey mate, love yer work, here’s a couple of bucks, good on ya!”. So I’m throwing my hat into the ring on the side of the “Yep, have a ‘buy me a coffee’ button” group. If you look around my blog, you’ll see a buy me a coffee button at the bottom of my articles. I don’t get much money through those links. If anything, I’ve received all of about 10 € over the blog’s entire lifetime. It’s definitely not enough to cover my hosting costs. That doesn’t matter. What does matter is that each time someone drops me a tip via the buy-me-a-coffee button, I am absolutely overjoyed . Someone read an article! It was useful to them! And they liked it! Wicked! It’s brilliant. It’s feedback. Something I’ve written was valuable to someone! Yay! [insert short dance in front of laptop] I rarely get emails about my blog articles. Most responses have come from someone giving a tip and saying, “Hey, nice article”. That’s so cool! It’s not money I can live off (otherwise I’d be living under a bridge ); it’s a signal, it’s feedback, and it’s one of the small pieces of connection I get from the wider world after having put my thoughts and experience online. Yes, most of the stuff I write is for me (or more realistically, for my future self). Yet, when I write, I often have some imaginary “reader” in mind–someone who is going to benefit from the knowledge or experience I’m documenting. articles.title: Slightly better interpolating spline
articles.content: Slightly better interpolating spline. Today I'm introducing a new interpolating spline. Its name is S9. Without further demagoguery, here it is - You can click on knots and drag to see how this thing works. For comparison with other splines, here is a demo. And here you can find the implementation source. Why automatic spline at all? For decades people were used to manually clicking and dragging cubic Bézier points until they developed Stockholm syndrome for it. Sometimes experienced designers will even tell you about having some magic rules like "keeping control arm lengths to about a third of chord length" which is good advice, but only if no better option is available. The fact is, humans cannot manually come up with good looking sequences of curves. The problem is inability to see subtle variations in the curvature of polynomial curves. So what is this curvature anyway? The best way to explain is using a related concept called osculating circle . It is an approximation of how the curve is bending at any point on it. Take a look at this demo - If you play with this for long enough, you will see a pattern. If a circle size along the curve changes very little, the curve looks better. If it changes a lot, the curve looks worse. This smoothness of how the circle changes along the curve is called curvature variation. Less variation is better. We can visualise this in a different way. If we record the reciprocal of osculating circle radius on every step of the curve, we get curvature profile of a curve. Now you can see another pattern. If this plot is smooth, the curve also looks smooth. However, it can be very difficult to see how smooth or not smooth this blue function is. Especially in absence of large spikes and multiple turns. Instead, let me show you another related plot. Here, in red, is a plot of a function representing curvature variation of the curve. And the rule is simple - thinner this plot gets, less curvature variation the curve has. We want the red part to be as close to the horizontal grey line as possible. For example, a section of a circle will have an integral (red number next to function plot) of this function equal to zero. As you can see, it can be quite hard to get this red function to relax. But it can still be worse though. This is just one segment. How about we connect two curves? See now you have to juggle more than two balls - you need to make individual curves smooth, but also keep the connection between the curves continuous too. In other words, the blue function must not have any gaps and the red function must stay as flat as possible. This gets worse with every additional curve because polynomial curves have this property where changing one side of it will change curvature on the other side as well. At this point you should see that trying to get harmony out of 20 or 30 connected curves has the same entertainment value as colonoscopy. This is what splines solve. articles.title: What's new in Node.js 27
articles.content: On October 29, 2026, the Node.js team published v27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0 . If you have been using Node.js for a few years, that version string alone probably made you do a double take. Where is the usual October v27.0.0 Current release? Node.js 27 is the first release to follow the new annual schedule. Under the old schedule, October brought a major release that reached end of life six months later without entering Long Term Support (LTS). October now starts a six-month Alpha phase, ahead of the 27.0.0 Current release in April 2027 and LTS promotion in October 2027. Wait, an odd-numbered Node.js release becoming LTS? Yes, the odd/even split is gone. Version numbers now match the calendar year (27 in 2027), with one major release per year, and every release becomes LTS. We covered the timeline and the reasons for the change in Node.js is changing its release schedule and version numbers . Because Node.js 27 is currently in its Alpha window, I will keep updating this article as new builds land on the way to April 2027. In this first Alpha, V8 moves from 14.6 to 15.6, adding Iterator.zip() , Iterator.zipKeyed() , Iterator.prototype.join() , Iterator.prototype.includes() , and Math.sumPrecise() . There is a promises API for node:net , along with async-iterable TCP servers. The Virtual File System ( node:vfs ) is now unflagged, the Permission Model gains --allow-env , and HTTP and memory defaults change too. We’ll start with the JavaScript and Node.js APIs you can use in everyday code, comparing them with the older approaches. Then we’ll cover runtime changes and what to check before upgrading. Quick Answer: what’s new in Node.js 27 The main additions in Node.js 27 so far: New Iterator helpers ( zip , zipKeyed , join , includes ) pair sequences, join their values into strings, and search them without collecting intermediate arrays. Math.sumPrecise() sums an iterable of numbers without rounding each intermediate addition. node:net/promises and async-iterable net.Server let you use async / await to set up TCP servers and sockets. Virtual File System ( node:vfs ) is unflagged, making in-memory file systems and --vfs-load available without --experimental-vfs . Core upgrades across fs , permissions, test runner, and http , including atomic temp files with fs.mkstemp() , --allow-env , Jest-style mock helpers, and a 65-second HTTP keepAliveTimeout . V8 15.6 and OpenSSL 4.1 update sorting and cryptography, and the default heap limit rises to 4 GB on an 8 GB machine. For example, we can format a list of products and total their prices: const items = [ ' Keyboard ' , ' Mouse ' , ' Monitor ' ] const prices = [ 129.99 , 49.99 , 349.95 ] const lines = Iterator . zipKeyed ( { item : items , price : prices } ) . map ( ({ item , price }) => ` ${ item } ($ ${ price . toFixed ( 2 ) } ) ` ) console . log ( ` ${ lines } -> Total: $ ${ Math . sumPrecise (prices) } ` ) // Keyboard ($129.99), Mouse ($49.99), Monitor ($349.95) -> Total: $529.93 If you want to experiment locally,

articles.title: vercel-labs/agent-browser (Rust)
articles.content: Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell. agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. snapshot returns the page as compact text with a ref such as @e1 for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call. npm install -g agent-browser agent-browser install # download Chrome for Testing (first time only) Homebrew: brew install agent-browser , then agent-browser install . Linux: agent-browser install --with-deps also installs the browser's system libraries. No install: npx agent-browser open example.com . Project installs, building from source, upgrade , and doctor are covered in Installation . agent-browser open example.com agent-browser snapshot -i # interactive elements, each with a ref agent-browser click @e1 # act on a ref from that snapshot agent-browser get url # check the result agent-browser close The snapshot for example.com : - link "Learn more" [ref=e1] Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again. CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example agent-browser find role button click --name "Submit" . See Selectors . A click fails, instead of reporting success, when the target is hidden, disabled, outside the viewport, or covered by another element such as a consent banner. Dismiss the covering element, take a new snapshot, and retry. The full walkthrough is in the quick start . The CLI sends each command to a background daemon that starts on the first command and controls the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Each --session gets its own daemon and browser. By default, the daemon closes a headless browser and exits after one hour without commands, saving state first when session persistence is configured. Chrome for Testing is the default browser. You can also attach to a running Chrome with --cdp or --auto-connect ( CDP mode ), select the Lightpanda or Obscura engine with --engine , drive Mobile Safari in the iOS Simulator , or use a cloud browser provider such as Browserbase , Browserless , Browser Use , Kernel , or AgentCore . The CLI ships skills that match its version: agent-browser skills get core # the core loop, refs, waiting, and common workflows agent-browser skills get core --ref commands # one reference, such as the full command list agent-browser skills get core --full # adds the full command reference and templates agent-browser skills list # specialized skills: electron, slack, dogfood, and more Install the discovery skill into an agent harness from skills.sh : npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-browser The installed skill is a thin stub that tells the agent to load agent-browser skills get core , so its instructions always match the installed CLI. Its premise is that traditional software development infrastructure, particularly the pull request (PR) model, is not well suited to an environment where AI agents generate, review, and iterate on code at high speed. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: Entire推出专为人类开发者与AI编码智能体协作设计的Git平台，重新思考PR协作模式。

articles.title: Google Cloud Adds Self-Managed VMware Cloud Foundation on Bare Metal
articles.content: Google Cloud has made a self-managed VMware solution generally available, running VMware Cloud Foundation 9.x on dedicated Z3 bare metal with root access across ESXi, vCenter and NSX in 22 regions. It sits beside the Google-managed VMware Engine and matches customer-operated offerings from AWS and Oracle, shifting lifecycle, patching and Broadcom licensing back to the customer. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: 谷歌云在22个区域推出自管理VMware Cloud Foundation裸金属方案，与托管VMware Engine并存。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #542: AI week ahead: data center pause backers could win 15 governor races
articles.content: This issue is about the week ahead, and something is scheduled almost every day. On Tuesday, US voters choose 36 governors, and in up to 15 of those races the candidate who backs a pause on new data centers could win. Apple reports earnings today and AMD on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Apple starts testing Apple Intelligence in China with Alibaba's Qwen, and Agility Robotics expects to close its deal to go public. When Congress returns on November 9, OpenAI plans to push for "speed limits" on the most powerful AI. Last week, a fake Claude Code update reached up to 5,000 Cursor users, and in a Cornell and Yale test nine of ten AI models raised their own spending limits. In the middle: insuring Big Tech's debt now costs more than at any time since 2021.
articles.summary: AI周报：美国36场州长选举中，最多15场可能由支持暂停新建数据中心的候选人胜出。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: 微软、Alphabet、亚马逊本周将发布财报，投资者关注AI投入能否持续回报，CoreWeave债务违约保险成本飙升引发信贷市场担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: AI发现安全漏洞的速度已超过团队修复能力，部分公司AI智能体承担大量工作，测试智能体持续运行，企业AI应用进入新阶段。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 竞选团队和PAC在中期选举AI广告上花费超1.37亿美元，约70%未标注AI生成，最大亲AI超级PAC向空壳公司支付约2000万美元。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic警告小型AI模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备，引发对AI自主扩散风险的关注。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: 顶级AI模型在自主开展AI研究的测试中失败，专家关注AI能否独立做研究、治理话语权及军事与个人电脑应用。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI成本过高促使企业转向更便宜的模型，大规模部署已进入日常使用，同时AI受限或被移除的场景也在增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要优先事项，剑桥拒绝Turnitin新条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI使用已非未来议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: Meta的AI电话代理被曝背后有人工呼叫者介入，AI智能体的隐藏人工转接和隐私泄露问题浮出水面。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI实验室在未就故障报告达成一致前就发布智能体，私聊被阅读、模型写入自身记忆、插件静默更新等问题显现。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr提出Kerr定律，指出当前限制团队的核心是让所有人的心智模型与实际构建保持同步，尤其在智能体写代码时代。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens谈Postgres扩展生态，pg_lake引入DuckDB和Iceberg，讨论ETL痛点、Postgres 19及AI对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha谈将无聊的邮件服务扩展至300万用户，揭秘Go重写、面向智能体构建、pricing.md与MCP实践。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw 作者 Gavriel Cohen 讲述 40 小时周末项目如何成为爆红开源项目，并发展为一家企业级 AI 公司。

articles.title: Changelog IRL @ PlanetScale (Sept 17, 2026)
articles.content: Changelog is taking over PlanetScale's HQ We’re getting together IRL!! On Thursday, September 17th, Changelog is taking over PlanetScale’s HQ in San Francisco for an evening of short talks and conversations about AI, developer tools and what people are building. We’ll have a few conversations with special guests and time for questions, food, drinks and hanging out. I’ll be joined by three builders pushing this idea forward, starting with Dan Robinson from Detail (detail.dev), with more guests to be announced very soon. I also have 80 limited edition t-shirts printed to give away! This won’t be a few presentations followed by everyone heading home. We’re doing this Changelog-style: live conversations, questions from the room, drinks, and plenty of time afterward for the hallway track. If you’re in San Francisco, register to come hang out! Changelog IRL Thursday, September 17th, 2026 6:00pm – 9:00pm PDT PlanetScale HQ 108 Natoma St, San Francisco, CA 94105 Speakers Dan Robinson, (Detail) Christian Glassiognon, Developer Educator at PlanetScale TBD Schedule 6:00 - 6:45pm: Doors open, food, drinks and networking 6:45 - 7:00pm: Welcome and opening chat with Adam 7:00 - 8:00pm: Changelog IRL with Dan and special guests 8:00 - 8:15pm: Questions 8:30 - 9:00pm: Hanging out and networking 9:00pm: Close All times Pacific. PlanetScale HQ, 108 Natoma St, San Francisco.
articles.summary: Changelog 将于 9 月 17 日在 PlanetScale 旧金山总部举办线下活动，围绕 AI 与开发者工具展开分享交流。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com 联合创始人 Peer Richelsen 讨论将开源项目转为闭源，并提出多数开源仓库可能已被攻陷的观点。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale 推出 5 美元 Postgres 服务，介绍 Vitess 重做、代理提交 schema 变更及是否开源的考量。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst 创始人 Haroon Meer 介绍 Canary 蜜罐与数字绊线，用于检测攻击者触碰 AWS API 密钥等行为。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: Max Stoiber 讲述从 react-boilerplate 等开源项目到加入 OpenAI 负责 ChatGPT 插件目录与平台开发的经历。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.
articles.summary: Cloudflare 的 Matt Carey 介绍 Code Mode，让单个 MCP 服务器以约 1000 token 暴露约 2500 个 API 端点。

articles.title: FDA Warns GLP-1s May Increase Risk of Sudden Blindness
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from NBC News: The Food and Drug Administration said Monday that GLP-1 drugmakers must add a warning label about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness. The condition, called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, affects the optic nerve, which carries signals from the eye to the brain. When blood flow to the nerve is reduced or blocked, it can cause sudden vision loss. The condition is permanent with no known treatment. The FDA said "there is a potential increased risk of rare NAION" in people taking GLP-1 drugs. The agency's requirement applies to all GLP-1s, including Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound, as well as several older GLP-1 diabetes medications. [...] Previous research has found that GLP-1 use may increase the risk of NAION, and Lilly has said it was aware of studies on the potential link. The FDA said it began looking into a possible link after a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology that found diabetes patients prescribed semaglutide were four times as likely to develop NAION as those not prescribed the drug. The agency said it reviewed reports of side effects submitted to its adverse event monitoring system and analyzed data from multiple clinical trials. Cases of NAION have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 drugs, the FDA found. However, FDA scientists were not able to identify a mechanism for how the drugs could increase the risk of the eye condition. Risk factors for NAION can overlap with conditions seen in people taking GLP-1 drugs, including Type 2 diabetes, obesity, sleep apnea and hypertension. "Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss," with GLP-1 use, the FDA said in the release. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: FDA 要求 GLP-1 药物厂商加注罕见眼病 NAION 警告标签，该病可致突发失明。

articles.title: Microsoft Took 31 Years to Let You Kill Windows 11's Sticky Keys Popup
articles.content: Microsoft is testing a Windows 11 option that lets users permanently disable the Sticky Keys and Filter Keys activation prompts directly from the pop-ups themselves, ending a 31-year-old annoyance without requiring a trip into Settings. Windows Latest reports: Sadly, the dialog is still the same aging Win32 window, but we spotted Microsoft's design boss replying under an X post reply about this, saying he is working on modernizing legacy dialogs. The popup might be annoying, but did you know that it exists because of a pinball game from 1995? [...] The change is in Build 26340.9882 (Experimental) and Build 26320.9876 (Beta), both released on November 6 and based on Windows 11 version 26H2. Microsoft says you can "choose not to be asked again" from the Sticky Keys and Filter Keys dialogs, but it's a Controlled Feature Rollout in Experimental, so you may not see it yet. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 微软测试 Windows 11 新选项，允许用户直接在弹窗中永久关闭粘滞键和筛选键提示，终结 31 年困扰。

articles.title: Trump Backs Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Amid Chinese Spy Affair Investigation
articles.content: President Donald Trump says the FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged by U.S. intelligence to have gathered information for Beijing. "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape," Trump said at a White House briefing. The Associated Press reports: Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes. "I did speak to him today just to see if he's feeling all right, how you're doing," Trump said. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy." Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Xi. "No, I don't think so," Trump said. "I mean, maybe. I'm sure President XI will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he's a very honorable man." Nvidia has launched its own independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Meanwhile, China has denied the allegations. "The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said during a regular news briefing Monday. Further reading: Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 特朗普称 FBI 正调查英伟达 CEO 黄仁勋与一名被指为中国搜集情报的女性之间的关系，并表示其应无大碍。

articles.title: Epic Games Comments On Planned Linux Distribution Support
articles.content: Epic Games says it plans to support its new Linux launcher on as many distributions as possible, specifically naming Fedora, SteamOS, CachyOS and Omarchy. GamingOnLinux's Liam Squires-Hand reports: Speaking to Jake Jones, Communications Director at Epic Games, they said: "Hey Liam! The new Epic Games Launcher is still in Preview and we plan to support as many Linux distributions as possible, including Fedora, SteamOS, Cachy, Omarchy, and more. We're testing and evaluating packaging formats for distribution, and we'll restore AppImage this month." With that in mind, until things settle down, you might see different packaging types appear or disappear until they decide firmly how they plan to support different distributions each with their own different packaging formats. Or, perhaps they might see the Flatpak light and just put it up officially on Flathub. Would make it even easier for SteamOS then too with Flathub, since it would just be a quick pop to Desktop Mode to install it directly in the Discover app. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Epic Games 表示其新 Linux 启动器将支持 Fedora、SteamOS、CachyOS 和 Omarchy 等多个发行版。

articles.title: France Accuses Iran of Supermarket Fridge Hacking
articles.content: France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of being behind last month's cyberattacks on fridges and freezers across the country. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions "at the European level." The BBC reports: The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up, which spoilt fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros. Then last week, dozens of supermarkets across several other European countries were also impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted fridges and freezers. It is not known if the instances are linked. Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people." He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act." France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it," Barrot added. Separately on Monday, the Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as well as his two deputies. Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC. Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime. [...] The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 法国指控伊朗革命卫队策划上月针对全国超市冷柜的大规模网络攻击，称其规模和攻击性前所未有。

articles.title: Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: Investigators at the Commerce Department were deep into a monthslong investigation of a Singaporean company that they suspected of smuggling Nvidia's artificial intelligence chips into China when their work came to a sudden halt late last year. The investigation centered on Megaspeed, a data center company led by an executive who U.S. officials now believe to be a Chinese spy who had a relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang. But the case was abruptly transferred to the Justice Department last year. The shift came after Commerce Department investigators working on the case received an email from Nvidia's general counsel seeking information about the inquiry into Megaspeed. It is not necessarily unusual for Commerce Department agents working on a case to speak with a company's representatives about issues involving their firm. But what was unusual was the content of the message. Tim Teter, Nvidia's general counsel, said that Jeff Kessler, a top official at the department, had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case. The agents were alarmed that Nvidia had invoked the name of Mr. Kessler, their superior, who was nominated to his role by President Trump. Some viewed Mr. Kessler's interaction with Nvidia as violating government procedure and potentially tainting the case, according to current and former government officials and others familiar with the incident. It is not clear what led to Mr. Teter's outreach to the department, but the recent revelations about Mr. Huang's acknowledged affair with a Megaspeed executive have only intensified scrutiny of Nvidia's role in influencing policy on chip sales to China. [...] The incident raised questions about what Mr. Kessler, who reports directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, had discussed with Nvidia. It also raised the possibility that those discussions could become their own subject of inquiry. Perhaps inadvertently, some offi
articles.summary: 美商务部对一家新加坡公司涉嫌走私英伟达 AI 芯片至中国的调查，在英伟达介入后突然中止。

articles.title: Google Unveils Two New Specialized AI Chips to Widen Its Challenge to Nvidia
articles.content: Google is expanding its AI chip lineup with two specialized TPUs arriving next year: the TPU 8tx, which encrypts sensitive data at the chip level for confidential computing, and the TPU 8i Max, which combines two TPU chips to provide more processing power and memory for long-context workloads. The move broadens Google's challenge to Nvidia as demand outstrips supply, with Google saying every TPU it currently has is already committed to customers. Quartz reports: The 8tx is designed for sensitive, privacy-focused jobs run by clients including public-sector bodies and businesses in heavily regulated sectors, according to Bloomberg. It pairs with a central processing unit from Advanced Micro Devices and encrypts data at the chip level. Normally, data must be decrypted in memory as the machine works on it, [said Amin Vahdat, Chief Technologist for AI & Infrastructure at Google]. The 8i Max is meant for AI applications that need long context windows, meaning the volume of information a model can take into account within one request. Vahdat said that matters for drug discovery, math and coding. The chip packs two TPU chips together, giving it extra processing muscle and memory. Both variations are reconfigured versions of existing silicon rather than new designs, Vahdat said. Google changed them to handle tasks customers have requested. They follow two TPU models Google released this year, according to Bloomberg, which said the chip unit used to release one new processor every two years. "We could build a single chip that tries to address the whole market, or by building specialized versions of the chips, we actually can deliver much more value," Vahdat said, according to Bloomberg. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 谷歌发布两款专用 TPU：面向机密计算的 TPU 8tx 和面向长上下文负载的 TPU 8i Max，明年推出。

articles.title: Huawei Says It's Made a 100% Chinese PC
articles.content: Huawei has unveiled the Qingyun HM650, a desktop PC it claims is made entirely from Chinese-manufactured components, including its own 10-core Kirin X90 processor and an enterprise version of HarmonyOS. "While Huawei has reportedly claimed local companies manufactured 100 percent of the components in the machine, it is unclear if all those components use Chinese designs," notes The Register. From the report: A single Chinese government agency has reportedly signed up for 600 of the machines. That's not an indication this machine is a curiosity, because Beijing has ordered all government entities to shift from Wintel boxes to local alternatives. [...] Even if Huawei is using some parts that aren't entirely Chinese, the debut of the Qingyun HM650 is bad news for Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm, as all are suffering as the PC market shrinks due to the rising cost of memory. China's government is an enormous buyer, and losing the chance to bid for its business is unlikely to be helpful. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 华为发布青云 HM650 台式机，称全部采用中国制造组件，搭载自研 10 核麒麟 X90 与企业版鸿蒙。

articles.title: Reddit Founder Says Building Social Media Apps Is 'Not Cool Anymore'
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Alexis Ohanian wants to figure out the future of user-generated content. According to the Reddit cofounder, building social media apps is "not cool anymore" and so much of the internet has been compromised. "I'm expecting some better version of the group chat to be that new version of UGC," Ohanian told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the inaugural WIRED World Fair. [...] Ohanian is a proponent of the "Dead Internet Theory"—the idea that a lot of online activity and content is being generated by bots. Large language models have turbocharged this, with AI agents outrunning human users. "The internet that I grew up on that was really built for humans first; user interfaces and experiences are going to go away," said Ohanian, "because more of the internet is going to get created for these agents to use, [rather] than for people." In some ways, the advance in generative AI has been lucrative for sites like Reddit, which has licensed its vast archive of human conversations to companies including Google and OpenAI to train AI models. "Platforms like ours became very, very valuable to LLMs," Ohanian said. But the technology has also undermined the business. Reddit shares plunged 29 percent last week after the platform warned that Google's AI-powered search was hurting referral traffic. Ohanian also worries the commercialization of these conversations means they are full of "bullshit." "The internet has gotten so manipulated because it is so incredibly valuable to do so," he said. Reddit recently said it would require users to sign in to fight third-party scraping and keep up user engagement. While Ohanian declined to say whether he agrees with the move, "there has to be provable humanity on the internet without being creepy." An early Anthropic investor, Ohanian is nonetheless optimistic about the potential benefits of AI. He is especially excited to see medical breakthroughs from the technology. "There is still a

articles.title: pathmask matches relative paths against patterns in the syntax of .gitignore
articles.content: Match relative paths against patterns in the syntax of .gitignore . pathmask checks paths as text and never reads the file system. Use it to filter a list of files the way git does. Required Node.js 22 or newer. The mask matches logs except keep.log , and the folder tmp with all its content: import { PathMask } from 'pathmask' ; const mask = new PathMask ( [ '*.log' , '!keep.log' , 'tmp/' ] ) ; mask . matches ( 'error.log' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'keep.log' ) ; // false mask . matches ( 'tmp/' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'tmp/cache/a.json' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'src/index.js' ) ; // false Creates a mask from the lines of a .gitignore file. Parameter Type Description patterns string[] The lines of the mask, see Patterns and Lines . Throws a TypeError when patterns is not an array of strings. Checks one path. Parameter Type Description path string A path relative to the root of the mask, see Paths . Returns true when the mask matches the path or a folder that contains it. Throws a TypeError when the path is empty, starts with / , or has an empty part, . or .. . The constructor reads the patterns, matches() only checks the path. Create one mask and use it for all paths: const ignored = new PathMask ( [ 'node_modules/' , '*.log' , '.*' ] ) ; const paths = [ 'README.md' , 'debug.log' , '.env' , 'src/index.js' , 'node_modules/ansis/index.js' ] ; const files = paths . filter ( ( file ) => ! ignored . matches ( file ) ) ; // ['README.md', 'src/index.js'] Filter the files of a folder This example reads all files of the folder my-project and its subfolders, then keeps the files that the mask does not match. The folder has the same files as the list above. import { readdir } from 'node:fs/promises' ; import path from 'node:path' ; import { PathMask } from 'pathmask' ; const rootPath = './my-project' ; const ignored = new PathMask ( [ 'node_modules/' , '*.log' , '.*' ] ) ; const entries = await readdir ( rootPath , { recursive : true , withFileTypes : true } ) ; const files = [ ] ; for ( const entry of entries ) { if ( ! entry . isFile ( ) ) continue ; // PathMask needs a path relative to the root. const file = path . relative ( rootPath , path . join ( entry . parentPath , entry . name ) ) ; if ( ! ignored . matches ( file ) ) { files . push ( file ) ; } } // ['README.md', 'src/index.js'] A mask can also pick the files to keep. Here the mask matches the JavaScript files of src and all Markdown files: const selected = new PathMask ( [ 'src/**/*.js' , '*.md' ] ) ; const paths = [ 'README.md' , 'docs/guide.md' , 'package.json' , 'src/index.js' , 'src/cli/run.js' , 'test/run.test.js' ] ; const files = paths . filter ( ( file ) => selected . matches ( file ) ) ; // ['README.md', 'docs/guide.md', 'src/index.js', 'src/cli/run.js'] With /*.md only the Markdown files of the root are matched: README.md , without docs/guide.md . A path is relative to the root of the mask, with / between its parts. A folder ends with / . Path Is README.md a file in the roo

articles.title: Announcing Parcel 3 Alpha
articles.content: Announcing Parcel 3 alpha 2026-11-04 Today we're releasing the first alpha of Parcel 3, a ground up rewrite of Parcel in Rust. It is up to 100x faster than v2, and supports native plugins written in Rust, Go, Swift, or C, as well as a custom runtime for JavaScript and TypeScript plugins. It also includes improved automatic code splitting, library mode, tree shaking, centralized configuration, and much more. Why a rewrite? In Parcel v2, we rewrote several individual pieces of Parcel in Rust. First was our JavaScript compiler , built on top of SWC. Then, we built Lightning CSS . Later, we rebuilt our HTML and SVG transformer and optimizers. However, Parcel's core was still written in JavaScript. This limited our maximum possible performance due to lack of shared memory between threads, high memory usage, garbage collection, and the cost of serializing values between workers and languages. Parcel v3 is an entirely self-contained Rust binary, with no dependency on Node at all. Everything from the CLI and dev server, to the transformers, bundler, optimizers, and everything in between is now fully native. This enables us to efficiently take full advantage of modern multi-core hardware. The results speak for themselves: up to 100x faster builds using the same underlying compilers as v2, only changing the core. Performance Let's cut to the benchmarks. Here's a comparison of cold development builds between v2 and v3 for React Spectrum , a large TypeScript monorepo. For reference: Storybook : ~100 entries, JS macros , custom plugins ported to Rust for Parcel 3. Docs website : ~340 pages, React Server Components, MDX, Tailwind, custom plugins. Library build : ~160 packages, TSX, macros, CSS modules, SVG icons. Outputs over 14,000 files. Development build time Cold development build time, Parcel 2 vs Parcel 3 Storybook: Parcel 2 16.62s, Parcel 3 572ms (29× faster). Docs website: Parcel 2 87.59s, Parcel 3 810ms (108× faster). Library build: Parcel 2 131.47s, Parcel 3 2.71s (49× faster). Storybook Storybook – Parcel 2: 16.62s 16.62s Storybook – Parcel 3: 572ms (29× faster) 572ms · 29× faster Docs website Docs website – Parcel 2: 87.59s 87.59s Docs website – Parcel 3: 810ms (108× faster) 810ms · 108× faster Library build Library build – Parcel 2: 131.47s 131.47s Library build – Parcel 3: 2.71s (49× faster) 2.71s · 49× faster Parcel 2 Parcel 3 Memory usage Memory usage, Parcel 2 vs Parcel 3 Storybook: Parcel 2 7.7GB, Parcel 3 1.5GB (5.1× less). Docs website: Parcel 2 13.9GB, Parcel 3 2.1GB (6.6× less). Library build: Parcel 2 5.7GB, Parcel 3 2.3GB (2.5× less). Storybook Storybook – Parcel 2: 7.7GB 7.7GB Storybook – Parcel 3: 1.5GB (5.1× less) 1.5GB · 5.1× less Docs website Docs website – Parcel 2: 13.9GB 13.9GB Docs website – Parcel 3: 2.1GB (6.6× less) 2.1GB · 6.6× less Library build Library build – Parcel 2: 5.7GB 5.7GB Library build – Parcel 3: 2.3GB (2.5× less) 2.3GB · 2.5× less Parcel 2 Parcel 3 Speed without caching In Parcel 2, we heavily invested in disk
